![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14146835/assets/01a5f06674cacca4764f438a8c06f020659f0177a0b74952f40bc9072627ec3f.png)

Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2},$ where 

- ${C}_{1}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{1}(t)=2{t}^{2}\,i-{t}^{3}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1],$ and

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=2\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=4t\,i-3{t}^{2}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}y\,dx-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-{t}^{3})\cdot 4t\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}t\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & =4[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{cos}^{3}⁡t,\,{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }9{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14146835/assets/ef44f01fb462cdf608f66a60dd11b8df798603bd204dca9d579ed50b370a84e3.png)

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $r(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j$ 
for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\cdot (-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡2t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$
